No, that isn't right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own.

**Example.** A student tells the assistant on Monday, "I finished the laser cutter safety training." On Thursday they open a new chat and ask, "Can I book the laser cutter?" The model has never seen Monday's message. Each time you call it, it sees only the text you send in that call, which is the **context**: your instructions, the conversation so far, and any tool results. Nothing carries over from one call to the next.

**Why it seems otherwise.** Chat apps hide the work. They store the conversation and send the whole history back to the model on every turn, so it looks like the model remembers. If the app stops sending the history, the model forgets.

**For your assistant,** memory is something you build:
- Save what matters between sessions, such as each student's training status, in a database or file.
- Load the relevant part into the context at the start of a session, or give the assistant a tool to look it up.

That makes it a design choice. Everything you load costs tokens (the units models read and bill by), so you'll have to decide what to keep, with your budget in mind.

Quick check: if the assistant needs to know a student's training status on Thursday, what two things must your code do?

I can turn this into a short lesson on context and memory, the next step in your mission, if you'd like one.
